presentation.title: Sweepstakes / Prize Advance-Fee Scam
presentation.summary: An official-looking notice claims a $50,000 prize. A warm prize representative gradually turns excitement into requests for sensitive information, an upfront fee, secrecy, and additional payments.
presentation.practiceGoal: Recognize that real prizes do not require upfront payment, confirm that you entered the exact sweepstakes, and verify the exact sponsor independently before sharing information or money.

warningSigns.sign: The learner did not verify entering the exact sweepstakes.
The unsolicited notice promised a large prize and imposed a 48-hour claim deadline.
The sponsor name was vague, and no exact independently verified sponsor was found.
A similarly named business was not the same organization.
The claim number, seal, certificate, signature, employee ID, and legal-looking language came from the same unverified operation.
The supplied website, phone number, and mail-processing address repeated the operation's own claims.
The representative used celebration and questions about future plans to build emotional commitment.
The claim form requested unnecessary identity, bank, card, and identification information.
The representative demanded taxes, processing, insurance, delivery, or release fees before prize delivery.
The representative refused to deduct the supposed fee from the supposed winnings.
The payment recipient, Daniel Cross, did not match the supposed sponsor.
Gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps, cryptocurrency, cashier's checks, and courier cash were major warning signs.
A smaller test or good-faith payment was still a loss.
Secrecy and a bank cover story separated the learner from protective outside advice.
Additional fees and fee-recovery offers continued the same advance-fee pattern.

finalReview.safestAction: Do not pay to receive a prize. Verify that you entered the exact sweepstakes, locate the sponsor independently, and discuss any fee or sensitive-information request with someone trusted before acting.

realWorldActions.action: Stop contact, block the sender, and preserve the notice, website, messages, call details, certificates, and fee documents.
If contact information was shared, review privacy settings and expect targeted prize, charity, banking, or identity messages.
If identity information was shared, use legitimate identity-theft protection and reporting resources and review financial or credit activity.
If bank or card information was shared, contact the real financial institution immediately through a trusted number and explain exactly what was disclosed.
If money was sent, contact the relevant bank, card issuer, payment provider, check issuer, gift-card issuer, or other legitimate institution immediately and ask what actions may still be available.
Tell someone trusted, report the prize operation through legitimate channels, and avoid anyone promising guaranteed recovery for another upfront fee.

artifact.heading: Simulated Bright Future Celebration Sweepstakes notice
artifact.message: "Congratulations! You have won $50,000. Call to claim within 48 hours." The unsolicited notice displays a gold-colored seal, a prize-director signature, fictional claim number BF-EXAMPLE-50000, a supplied phone number and website, small print, and a warning that failure to respond forfeits the prize. It does not show when or how you entered.

artifact.transcript: A clearly simulated official-looking letter or email announces a fifty-thousand-dollar prize from the fictional Bright Future Celebration Sweepstakes. It says, "Congratulations! You have won $50,000. Call to claim within 48 hours." It includes a gold-colored seal described in text, a prize-director signature, fictional claim number BF-EXAMPLE-50000, a supplied phone number, a supplied website, and small print saying the prize will be forfeited. The notice does not show when or how the learner entered. The visual deadline does not control learner response time.

artifact.transcript: A simulated phone call connects to fictional Elaine Mercer, Senior Prize Claims Coordinator. Elaine warmly says, "This is a wonderful day for you. I am honored to confirm that your claim number has been selected for the $50,000 grand prize." She repeats the claim number printed on the notice, gives a fictional employee ID, says the call is recorded and the prize is insured, and refers to legal and tax departments. She asks what the learner plans to do with the money, whether anyone else knows, for contact information, and whether electronic deposit is possible.
